answer: The sailmaker cuts each sail from the loft's canvas and records the sail, the ship and the cloth in his book, so every sail is proved cut to measure. A wharf sail claimed as cut fails the record: the cloth must match the loft's own bolt at the tide of the cutting, and a sail never cut is no more than cloth on the roll. Buying a false sail record costs 15,300 in bribes to the sailmaker and a forged stamp, and the glacier book is read at every fitting, so a sail whose cut was never recorded is left in the loft.
